newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Death toll from haj blaze in Saudi rises to 343.
newsitem.headline: Death toll from haj blaze in Saudi rises to 343.

text.p: The death toll of Moslem haj pilgrims rose to 343 on Wednesday in the aftermath of a huge fire at a temporary camp in Saudi Arabia, official Saudi media said.

The media did not give new figures for the number of people injured when Tuesday's blaze tore through the tent camp at the plain of Mena, about 11 km (seven miles) from the Islamic holy city of Mecca. Officials had previously said 1,290 were injured in the fire.
Saudi radio said authorities were still struggling to identify the victims and determine their nationality.

The official media did not give a breakdown, but diplomats said earlier most of them were Indians, Pakistanis and Bangladeshis. Saudi newspapers said the fire had also engulfed Syrian, Lebanese, Egyptian, Sudanese, Yemeni and Moroccan sections of the camp.
Diplomats said identification was difficult as many bodies were severely burnt.
Victims of the fire had been rushed to 12 nearby hospitals, and specialised medical centres several hours away were on high alert in case seriously injured victims would be transferred.

Saudi television showed many of the victims in hospital beds, some of them old and frail, others young and afraid. One bandaged young child stared into the camera, its face distorted with pain. Many patients displayed their badly burnt bodies.
Saudi Arabia said the fire was an accident and had no political motive. Officials said the blaze, fanned by high winds, had whipped through 70,000 tents in Mena.

"Investigations indicate that the fire was an accident," Saudi Arabia's ambassador in London Ghazi Algosaibi said in a statement. "We are faced with a human tragedy which has no political implications."
Diplomats and witnesses said the blaze was caused by gas cylinder explosions but Riyadh gave no cause.
Diplomats said earlier they feared the death toll might rise from the fire, which had spread panic among thousands of pilgrims performing one of Islam's holiest rites.

In Mena on Wednesday, the air was still thick with the smell of smoke and the ground was littered with debris, such as burnt-out buses and charred water bottles. Trucks carted off blackened rubble, while workers -- helped by the Saudi army -- hurried to erect new tents.

While officials struggled to identify the dead, treat the injured and shelter pilgrims stranded by the blaze, a flood of pilgrims in seamless white robes scrambled up Mount Arafat where the Prophet Mohammed gave his last sermon 14 centuries ago.
Moslems traditionally sleep at the encampment in Mena before their trek to Mount Arafat, the pinnacle of an elaborate set of haj rituals.
Pilgrims marched to Mount Arafat with prayer rugs slung over their shoulders, carrying plastic water bottles and umbrellas to cope with the 40 Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) heat.
On their way, many chanted "I have answered your call, God, there is no God but you". A blind cleric held the traditional midday sermon at Arafat, but made no reference to the disaster.

Ambassador Algosaibi said: "The fire at Mena and the ensuing loss of life and the injuries is a tragedy for all Moslems. The custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, King Fahd bin Abdul-Aziz, expressed his sympathy and condolences to the families of the victims. It is a sentiment the whole Saudi people shares."
Some two million Moslems prayed at Mount Arafat, marking the the peak of haj.
Pilgrims will spend Wednesday night at Mozdalifah, between Mena and Mount Arafat, where they will collect pebbles to stone three pillars symbolising the devil.
On Thursday, Moslems around the world celebrate Eid al-Adha (Feast of Sacrifice) at the end of haj.

The blaze was the latest tragedy to strike the pilgrimage to Mecca. Able-bodied Moslems are obliged to make haj at least once if they can afford it. In 1990, 1,426 pilgrims were crushed to death in a stampede in a tunnel and in 1994, 270 pilgrims died in another stampede.
